relationships.description: The jointly performed infrastructure exchange reads or writes a concrete file or data unit during its execution, such as a replication sync shipping write-ahead-log segments or a consensus round persisting a snapshot file.
relationships.evidence: The cluster software's configuration or source names the artifact path (e.g. a WAL directory, snapshot file or shared config document) that the coordination protocol reads or writes while the peers execute the interaction.

relationships.description: The collaborative exchange is an integral part of a broader ongoing infrastructure capability and has no independent existence outside it, as when a peer replication handshake exists only as a constituent of the data replication function.
relationships.evidence: Product or architecture documentation describes the function (e.g. replication or failover) as including this multi-peer protocol step, and the protocol code lives inside the module that implements that function.

relationships.description: The result or control state produced by one joint peer exchange is passed on to start or feed a subsequent joint exchange, as when a leader election hands the elected leader identity to the following log replication round.
relationships.evidence: Protocol code or design documentation shows the output of the first coordination phase (e.g. an elected term or prepared transaction ID) being passed as input to the second multi-peer protocol phase.

relationships.description: The joint peer behavior gives concrete operational form to the cooperating group of nodes or system software instances, since the collaboration exists precisely to carry out this exchange.
relationships.evidence: The cluster membership configuration (e.g. a Raft peer list or Galera wsrep_cluster_address) defines the peer group whose members execute the coordination protocol together.

relationships.description: The collaborative peer exchange is the behavior that actually delivers an externally visible infrastructure capability, such as a distributed commit protocol delivering a strongly consistent database service to consumers.
relationships.evidence: Service documentation or an SLA states that the offered capability (e.g. highly available storage or consistent key-value access) is provided by the cluster's quorum, replication or failover protocol.

relationships.description: Completion or failure of the joint peer exchange produces a discrete infrastructure state change, such as a finished leader election emitting a leader-changed event or a failed handover raising a failover alert.
relationships.evidence: The cluster software's source, logs or alerting rules show a named event or notification (e.g. 'leader_elected', 'failover_completed') being emitted at the end of the coordination protocol.

relationships.description: The outcome of the joint peer exchange starts an ordered automated workflow on a node or system software, as when a completed failover handover kicks off a DNS repointing or connection-pool reconfiguration procedure.
relationships.evidence: A hook, callback or orchestration script (e.g. a Patroni on_role_change callback or Pacemaker resource agent) is configured to launch the process when the coordination protocol completes.

relationships.description: The participating peers carry out their joint exchange by communicating through a specific protocol endpoint, such as a cluster peer port or replication listener exposed by each member.
relationships.evidence: The cluster configuration declares the peer or replication endpoint (e.g. etcd listen-peer-urls, a gossip port or a replication socket) over which members exchange the protocol messages, and firewall or security-group rules open that port between peers.

notes: realizes→TechnologyCollaboration is semantically wrong: behavior does not realize active structure; in ArchiMate the collaboration is assigned to the interaction (use assigned-to inverse). composes→TechnologyFunction is questionable: a function is performed by a single node, so a multi-participant interaction being part of it conflicts with both definitions; aggregation or flow fits better.
